title: The trophy of Mezentius' arms
greek: ingentem quercum decisis undique ramis / constituit tumulo fulgentiaque induit arma, / Mezenti ducis exuvias, tibi magne tropaeum / bellipotens
short: Aeneas dresses a lopped oak on a mound in Mezentius' armour and dedicates it to Mars: the classic description of a Roman-Greek battle trophy.
body: A tropaeum (Greek tropaion, from tropē, the 'turning' of the enemy) was a monument set up where the enemy was routed: a tree-trunk or post dressed in captured armour. Conington and Nettleship call this passage the locus classicus for the construction of a trophy: the trunk stands for the body of the beaten foe, with crest, broken spears, the corslet pierced in twelve places, the shield tied to the 'left hand' and the sword hung from the 'neck'. Aeneas himself makes the identification: 'my hands have set Mezentius here' (11.16). Servius adds that trophies were placed on high ground, and that Aeneas sets up a trophy rather than claiming a triumph because his victory is not yet complete; he also notes that 'magne ... bellipotens' names Mars by epithets alone. The scene fulfils the pattern of Pallas' vow to the Tiber (10.421-3) and inverts Mezentius' vow to make Lausus a trophy of Aeneas (10.774-6).

title: Pallas on the bier like a plucked flower
greek: qualem virgineo demessum pollice florem / seu mollis violae seu languentis hyacinthi
short: Pallas lying on his bier is like a violet or drooping hyacinth picked by a girl: its beauty remains, but the earth no longer feeds it.
body: The flower cut down is an old image for young death. Conington and Nettleship trace this version to Catullus' wedding song, where a flower 'plucked by a slender nail' loses its bloom (Catullus 62.39-44), and compare Propertius 1.20.39-40; Virgil had used a related image of Euryalus dying like a purple flower cut by the plough (9.435-7), itself echoing Catullus 11.21-4 and Homer's drooping poppy for the dying Gorgythion (Iliad 8.306-8). The phrase 'virgineo pollice' (by a maiden's thumb) adds a note of unfulfilled marriage, apt for a youth who died unwed. The hyacinth also recalls the myth of Hyacinthus, the boy loved and accidentally killed by Apollo, from whose blood the flower sprang. The simile softens the brutal account of Pallas' death in Book X into elegy.

title: Dido's robes as Pallas' shroud
greek: tum geminas vestis auroque ostroque rigentis / extulit Aeneas, quas illi laeta laborum / ipsa suis quondam manibus Sidonia Dido / fecerat
short: Aeneas wraps Pallas in one of two gold-stiffened purple robes that Dido once wove for him, linking his two great losses.
body: Conington and Nettleship explain that the robes are purple stiffened with gold embroidery, comparing the gifts Aeneas brought for Dido in 1.648-55. In Carthage Aeneas wore a cloak that Dido had woven with gold thread (4.262-4); now the last of her handiwork becomes a shroud. The detail 'laeta laborum' (happy in her work) recalls a time before the disaster of Book IV. Commentators have long discussed what the gesture means: grief that joins Dido and Pallas, both victims of Aeneas' mission; an honour fit for a prince; and, for some readers, an unsettling reminder that Aeneas' loves end in funerals. A similar gift-garment links generations in 3.482-91, where Andromache gives Ascanius robes she wove 'as a memorial of my hands'. The second robe veils the hair 'destined to the fire'.

title: Aethon, Pallas' horse, weeps in the procession
greek: post bellator equus positis insignibus Aethon / it lacrimans guttisque umectat grandibus ora
short: Pallas' war-horse walks stripped of its trappings and weeping, a detail from Homer and from Roman military funerals.
body: Servius explains that it was military custom to lead the dead man's horse to the tomb, without its trappings (phalerae), while his armour-bearer carried his arms reversed; Virgil, he says, preserves that custom. Conington and Nettleship compare the Roman practice of laying aside insignia in mourning (Tacitus, Annals 3.4). The weeping horse comes from Iliad 17.426-40, where Achilles' immortal horses weep for Patroclus; Servius adds that Pliny says the horse is the only animal besides man that weeps and feels grief, and Suetonius reports that horses wept before Caesar's death (Divus Iulius 81). The name Aethon ('Blazing') is borne by one of Hector's horses (Iliad 8.185) and, Servius notes, by a horse of the Dawn. The procession that follows also carries Pallas' spear and helmet, 'for all else is Turnus' prize', a pointed reminder of the sword-belt.

title: 'Versis armis': arms reversed in mourning
greek: tum maesta phalanx Teucrique sequuntur / Tyrrhenique omnes et versis Arcades armis
short: The Arcadians march with their weapons turned upside down, the soldier's sign of mourning.
body: Servius explains that mourners carried their spears with the butt, not the point, towards the ground, because 'our ancestors did everything contrary at a funeral'; he also reports a view, which he attributes to Bacchylides, that shields were turned over so that the images of gods painted on them would not be polluted by the sight of a corpse, and an alternative that shields were turned aside so that their emblems would not shine. Conington and Nettleship take 'versis' to mean inverted. The custom survives in military funerals today, where soldiers 'rest on arms reversed'. Here the Arcadians, Pallas' own countrymen, carry it out, so that the gesture marks them as the nearest mourners after the Trojans and Etruscans have passed.

title: 'Salve aeternum ... aeternumque vale'
greek: salve aeternum mihi, maxime Palla, / aeternumque vale
short: Aeneas' farewell to Pallas uses the ritual words spoken to the dead at Roman funerals: 'hail and farewell for ever'.
body: Romans took leave of the dead with the words salve and vale (or ave atque vale). Servius, quoted by Conington and Nettleship, cites Varro's Logistorici: these greetings are said to the dead not because they can be well or safe, but because we are leaving them and will never see them again. The most famous use is the close of Catullus' poem at his brother's tomb, 'atque in perpetuum, frater, ave atque vale' (101.10), which Virgil's 'aeternum' recalls. The formula is placed where Aeneas turns back to the war: 'the same dreadful destiny of war calls us hence to other tears'. Its brevity, after the long ceremonial procession, makes it one of the most moving moments of the book.

title: Latin envoys with olive branches ask for a burial truce
greek: iamque oratores aderant ex urbe Latina / velati ramis oleae veniamque rogantes
short: Envoys carrying wool-wreathed olive branches, the signs of suppliants and peace, ask leave to bury their dead; Aeneas grants it and offers peace to the living too.
body: Olive branches wound with wool were carried by suppliants and ambassadors seeking peace; Conington and Nettleship refer to their note on 7.154, where Aeneas sends envoys to Latinus 'all veiled with boughs of Pallas' olive'. The envoys ask that the dead be returned for burial, arguing that 'no war is waged with the conquered and the lifeless'. Recovery of the dead under truce was a recognised rule of ancient warfare (compare the truce for burying the dead in Iliad 7.394-432). Aeneas grants it with a striking addition: 'I would gladly grant peace to the living too' (equidem et vivis concedere vellem, 11.111). He insists that he came only because fate gave him this land, and that it was Latinus who broke faith; the war should be settled by single combat with Turnus, which anticipates Book XII.

title: Drances
greek: tum senior semperque odiis et crimine Drances / infensus iuveni Turno
short: The elderly Latin spokesman, Turnus' constant enemy, flatters Aeneas lavishly and promises to help build the walls of the new Troy.
body: Drances is Virgil's invention. As the oldest envoy he speaks for the rest (Conington compares Ilioneus in 1.521); 'odiis et crimine' means that he pursued Turnus with hatred and accusation, as Servius explains. His reply to Aeneas is an elaborate compliment ('shall I first admire thy justice or thy toils in war?') and ends with an extravagant offer: the Latins will gladly carry the stones of the 'walls of destiny'. Readers have always noticed that his praise of the enemy is coloured by his personal feud with Turnus. Virgil gives a fuller and very unflattering portrait of him in the council later in the book (11.336-42), where he attacks Turnus to his face and receives a furious reply.

title: The twelve days' truce
greek: bis senos pepigere dies, et pace sequestra / per silvas Teucri mixtique impune Latini / erravere iugis
short: Trojans and Latins agree a truce of twelve days to bury their dead, and mix peacefully in the woods while cutting timber for the pyres.
body: Conington and Nettleship compare Iliad 24.664-70, where Priam asks Achilles for eleven days to mourn and bury Hector, fighting to resume on the twelfth. 'Pace sequestra' uses a legal image: a sequester is a trustee or mediator who holds disputed property between two parties, so the peace 'stands between' the enemies for a time. The picture of former enemies wandering together in the forest is touching and ironic, since the war resumes almost at once. The felling of ash, pine, oak, cedar and rowan for the pyres repeats a set piece of epic: compare the cutting of wood for Patroclus' pyre (Iliad 23.114-22) and for Misenus' in Aeneid 6.179-82, which is often traced to a passage of Ennius' Annales.

title: The armed procession around the pyres (decursio)
greek: ter circum accensos cincti fulgentibus armis / decurrere rogos, ter maestum funeris ignem / lustravere in equis ululatusque ore dedere
short: Infantry and then cavalry ride three times round the burning pyres with a ritual cry, as the Myrmidons did for Patroclus and Roman armies did for fallen generals.
body: The verb 'decurrere' is the technical Roman word for a ceremonial armed parade (decursio) around the pyre of a commander. Conington and Nettleship cite the Homeric model, Iliad 23.13-14, where the Myrmidons drive their horses three times around Patroclus' body, and Appian's account of the funeral of the Lusitanian leader Viriathus, where infantry and cavalry ran round the pyre in arms. Livy reports that Hannibal gave the Roman general Ti. Sempronius Gracchus such a funeral (25.17.5). Three is the ritual number of purification ('lustravere'). The scene goes on with Roman and Homeric rites together: spoils and the dead men's own weapons thrown into the flames, cattle and pigs slaughtered, the watch kept over the embers until night. The Latins, by contrast, burn many of their dead 'uncounted and unhonoured'.

title: Diomedes at Argyripa (Arpi)
greek: ille urbem Argyripam patriae cognomine gentis / victor Gargani condebat Iapygis arvis
short: The envoys found Diomedes founding his city in Apulia, named after his native Argos; he refuses to join the Latins.
body: After the Trojan War Diomedes, king of Argos, did not return home but settled in Apulia (Iapygia), near Mount Garganus. His city, Argyripa, later called Arpi, was explained in antiquity as a corruption of 'Argos Hippion' (horse-rearing Argos): Conington and Nettleship note the derivation and the doubts about Arpi being a genuine Greek colony; Strabo discusses Diomedes' foundations in this region (6.3.9). The Latins had sent Venulus to ask his help in 8.9-17, hoping that Aeneas' old enemy would fight again. The answer, reported in direct speech (11.252-93), is the political turning point of the book: the greatest Greek warrior after Achilles refuses, warns the Latins against war with Aeneas, and advises peace. His speech also gives Virgil a chance to survey the miserable homecomings (nostoi) of the Greek heroes.

title: The Greek homecomings: Minerva's star, Caphereus, Proteus' Pillars
greek: scit triste Minervae / sidus et Euboicae cautes ultorque Caphereus ... Atrides Protei Menelaus adusque columnas / exsulat
short: Diomedes lists the disasters that met the victorious Greeks on their way home, as the gods' punishment for the sack of Troy.
body: Each item alludes to a story of the returns (Nostoi). 'Minerva's baleful star' is the storm Athena sent on the fleet because Locrian Ajax dragged Cassandra from her temple (compare 1.39-45). Caphereus is the cape of Euboea where Nauplius lit false beacons to wreck the Greeks, in revenge for the judicial murder of his son Palamedes; Conington and Nettleship note that Sophocles wrote a tragedy on the subject and that 'ultor' also suggests divine vengeance for Troy. Menelaus wandered to the 'Pillars of Proteus', the limits of Egypt, named on the analogy of the Pillars of Hercules (Odyssey 4.351-570; Herodotus 2.112-20 makes Proteus a king of Egypt). Ulysses saw the Cyclopes; Neoptolemus and Idomeneus lost their kingdoms; Agamemnon was murdered by his wife on his own threshold. The catalogue turns the victors into a 'band that even Priam might pity'.

title: Diomedes' companions turned into birds
greek: et socii amissi petierunt aethera pennis / fluminibusque vagantur aves
short: Diomedes' lost comrades have become sea-birds, a punishment he traces to his wounding of Venus at Troy.
body: The 'birds of Diomedes' (aves Diomedeae) were believed to live on the Diomedean islands off the coast of Apulia (the modern Tremiti), and to welcome Greeks and attack strangers. Conington and Nettleship explain that the birds 'follow' Diomedes even into exile, and refer to Heyne's excursus on them; they note that Virgil seems to confuse sea and river birds. Ovid tells the transformation at length (Metamorphoses 14.483-511), making it a punishment for a fresh insult to Venus during the wanderings. Virgil's Diomedes links his suffering to the moment he 'assailed celestial limbs with steel, and sullied the hand of Venus with a wound' (Iliad 5.330-43). The same episode was recalled by Venus herself in the council of Book X; the two passages frame the story of Diomedes in Italy.

title: 'Hic pietate prior': Diomedes' tribute to Aeneas
greek: ambo animis, ambo insignes praestantibus armis, / hic pietate prior
short: Diomedes, who fought Aeneas at Troy, ranks him with Hector in valour and above him in pietas, and advises the Latins to make peace.
body: This is the highest praise of Aeneas in the poem, and it comes from an enemy who 'met him hand to hand'. Hector and Aeneas, Diomedes says, held back the Greek victory until the tenth year; had Troy borne two more like Aeneas, the Trojans would have invaded Greece. Both were outstanding in courage and arms, 'this one first in pietas'. Conington and Nettleship find the first hint of Aeneas' piety in Iliad 20.297-9, where Poseidon says he always gave pleasing gifts to the gods; they note that in Iliad 24.66-70 Zeus speaks as warmly of Hector. In Iliad 6.77-9 Helenus calls Hector and Aeneas the best of the Trojans in battle and counsel. The phrase echoes 'pietate insignis et armis' (6.403). Diomedes' verdict sharpens the contrast with Turnus' later sneers at 'the effeminate Phrygian'.

title: The chair and the trabea: royal insignia
greek: et sellam regni trabeamque insignia nostri
short: Latinus proposes to send Aeneas gold, ivory, the royal chair and the striped robe, the insignia of kingship in early Latium.
body: Latinus' peace offer includes land, ships if the Trojans prefer to leave, a hundred envoys bearing olive branches, and gifts: gold, ivory, the chair (sella) and the trabea. The sella is the ivory seat of office that became the Roman curule chair; the trabea is a robe with purple stripes, worn in Roman antiquarian tradition by the early kings and by augurs and knights on ceremony (in 7.187-8 Picus wears it). Conington and Nettleship cross-refer to 7.188 and point out that the Romans themselves sent a purple robe and ivory chair to foreign kings they wished to honour, as Livy records for Syphax and Ptolemy (27.4). Virgil thus gives the Latin king a recognisably Roman diplomatic gesture. Lewis and Short define trabea as a robe of state with horizontal purple stripes.

title: Drances' character: 'largus opum et lingua melior'
greek: largus opum et lingua melior, sed frigida bello / dextera, consiliis habitus non futtilis auctor, / seditione potens
short: Virgil's portrait of Drances: rich, eloquent, cold in battle, a respected adviser and a skilled factional politician of doubtful paternal descent.
body: This compact character sketch introduces Drances' invective against Turnus in the council. Servius, cited by Conington and Nettleship, explains 'largus opum' as 'rich', not 'generous'. Conington adopts Heyne's view that Drances is 'a more respectable Thersites', perhaps a compound of Thersites, the abusive common soldier of Iliad 2.211-77, and Polydamas, Hector's prudent adviser; he also reports the old idea that Virgil had Cicero in mind, with Turnus as Mark Antony, and allows that it may be partly true since Drances, like Cicero, is a great orator with little military standing. Many modern critics resist so precise an identification. Drances' advice (give Lavinia to Aeneas; let Turnus fight alone) is in fact what the gods intend, yet Virgil makes the man who gives it unattractive, which complicates the reader's sympathies.

title: The Latin mothers' prayer to Pallas
greek: armipotens, praeses belli, Tritonia virgo, / frange manu telum Phrygii praedonis
short: Amata, Lavinia and the Latin women pray to Minerva to break the 'Phrygian robber's' spear: a close translation of a prayer in Iliad VI that the goddess refuses.
body: Conington and Nettleship note that these lines translate Iliad 6.305-7, where Theano and the Trojan women offer a robe to Athena and pray that she break the spear of Diomedes; Homer adds that Pallas Athene refused. Virgil's readers would know the ominous model, and the scene also echoes the Trojan women's vain prayer to Pallas pictured on Dido's temple (1.479-82). Tritonia refers to Lake Triton in Libya, associated with the goddess's birth. The roles are now reversed: the Latins are the besieged, and they call Aeneas 'the Phrygian plunderer', casting him as a second Paris who comes to steal a bride. Lavinia walks beside her mother, eyes lowered, 'the cause of so great an evil' (causa mali tanti), recalling Helen.

anchor: when a horse snaps his tether
title: Turnus like a horse breaking free
greek: qualis ubi abruptis fugit praesepia vinclis / tandem liber equus, campoque potitus aperto
short: Arming for battle, Turnus is compared to a stallion that breaks its tether and gallops to the pastures and river: an imitation of a famous Homeric simile for Paris.
body: Conington and Nettleship note that the simile is closely rendered from Iliad 6.506-11, used of Paris hurrying back to battle (and repeated for Hector at 15.263-8). They report that Ennius had already translated Homer's lines (quoted by Macrobius, Saturnalia 6.3), and that critics disagreed over whom the comparison suits better: Pope thought it more appropriate to Paris, Heyne to Turnus. Virgil adds the mares in the pasture and the familiar river, emphasising freedom, vanity and youthful energy. Coming straight after the Latin women's prayer, which casts Aeneas as Paris, the simile ironically gives Turnus the Homeric image of Paris; critics have read it as hinting at Turnus' exuberance and lack of restraint.

title: Metabus and the infant Camilla
greek: Priverno antiqua Metabus cum excederet urbe, / infantem fugiens media inter proelia belli / sustulit exsilio comitem
short: Diana tells how Camilla's father, expelled from Privernum, tied his baby to a spear, dedicated her to the goddess and hurled her across a flooded river.
body: Diana's story to her nymph Opis gives Camilla a mythical childhood. Metabus, a Volscian king driven out of Privernum for his tyranny, is trapped by the flooded Amasenus; he wraps the infant in cork bark, binds her to his oak spear, vows her to Diana as 'thine infant suppliant', and throws her over the stream before swimming after. She is raised in the wild on mare's milk, armed with javelin and bow, and dressed in a tiger skin instead of a gown, refusing marriage to remain Diana's virgin huntress. Servius, quoted by Conington and Nettleship, derives the name from Metabus, founder of Metapontum in southern Italy (compare Strabo 6.1.15). The upbringing recalls Greek huntress-heroines such as Atalanta. Diana's love makes Camilla's death inevitable and tragic: 'would she had not plunged thus into warfare!'

title: Casmilla / Camilla: 'attendant of the gods'
greek: nomine Casmillae mutata parte Camillam
short: Camilla's name, changed from her mother's name Casmilla, was understood in antiquity to mean a young attendant at sacrifices, fitting Diana's devotee.
body: Servius cites Statius Tullianus, who said that Callimachus reported that the Etruscans called Mercury 'Camillus', meaning the gods' attendant, so that Metabus well named his daughter Camilla as Diana's servant; he adds that Romans called noble boys and girls who assisted the flamens camilli and camillae, and quotes Pacuvius' 'caelitum camilla' of Medea. Conington and Nettleship note that Casmilus is generally taken as an older form of camillus, as Casmena is of Camena, and cite Varro, De lingua Latina 7.34, and Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.8. The etymology suits the story Diana is telling: Camilla was dedicated to the goddess before she could walk. The name also recalls the great Roman family of the Furii Camilli.

title: Opis, Diana's nymph
greek: velocem interea superis in sedibus Opim, / unam ex virginibus sociis sacraque caterva, / compellabat
short: Diana sends her companion Opis to avenge Camilla; she watches from a hill and shoots Camilla's killer Arruns.
body: Opis (or Upis) was a cult name connected with Artemis and with the Hyperborean maidens honoured at Delos (Herodotus 4.35). Conington and Nettleship note that her Thracian origin ('Threissa', 11.858) has not been mentioned before, and that Apollodorus names her as a Hyperborean; Servius says the Greeks told of Opis coming from the Hyperboreans (whom he counts as Thracians) to Latona and helping to rear Apollo and Diana, and that Virgil did not invent her. Diana gives her an arrow from her own quiver with the order that whoever, Trojan or Italian, wounds Camilla must pay with his blood. Opis keeps her charge: she watches 'undismayed' from the hilltops, laments Camilla's death in a short speech, and then shoots Arruns from the tomb of Dercennus, drawing the bow until the tips meet. Divine vengeance on the slayer of a favourite of the gods is an epic pattern; the death of Arruns, abandoned 'on the unknown dust', balances the honour Diana promises to Camilla.

title: Camilla the Amazon; Hippolyte and Penthesilea
greek: at medias inter caedes exsultat Amazon / unum exserta latus pugnae, pharetrata Camilla ... quales Threiciae cum flumina Thermodontis / pulsant
short: Camilla fights with one breast bared like an Amazon, and her women are compared to the Amazons of the Thermodon around Hippolyte or Penthesilea.
body: The Amazons, warrior women of Greek myth, lived on the river Thermodon in Pontus (northern Asia Minor). Hippolyte was the queen whose girdle Hercules took; Penthesilea fought for Troy and was killed by Achilles, and she already appears on Dido's temple frescoes 'with crescent shields' (1.490-3). Conington and Nettleship comment on 'unum exserta latus': Amazons were said to cut or burn off the right breast so that it did not hinder the bow, though in sculpture they are often shown with one breast simply bared; they compare 'exsertae mammae' of Penthesilea in 1.492. On the simile, Servius quotes a fragment of Sallust on the Amazons' plain of Themiscyra. Virgil's Camilla is an Italian Amazon: a picture of glamour and terror that ends, like Penthesilea's story, with the warrior maiden's death.

title: Camilla's companions: Larina, Tulla, Tarpeia
greek: Larinaque virgo / Tullaque et aeratam quatiens Tarpeia securim, / Italides
short: Camilla's bodyguard bear old Italian names; Tarpeia's recalls the Roman girl who betrayed the Capitol to the Sabines.
body: Virgil stresses that the women are 'Italides', daughters of Italy. Their names point to Roman legend: Tarpeia recalls the daughter of the commander of the Roman citadel who, in the story told by Livy (1.11.5-9), opened the citadel to the Sabines for a reward and was crushed under their shields; the Tarpeian Rock, from which traitors were thrown, bore her name. Giving that name to a loyal warrior of Camilla may be deliberate rehabilitation, a reminder of a darker future, or simply Italian colouring; commentators differ. Conington and Nettleship discuss whether all of Camilla's troops are women and conclude that she probably has only a small female staff, and they explain Tarpeia's bronze axe as the national weapon of the Italian countryfolk (compare 7.627).

title: The deceitful Ligurian, son of Aunus
greek: vane Ligus frustraque animis elate superbis, / nequiquam patrias temptasti lubricus artis
short: The son of Aunus tricks Camilla into dismounting and then gallops off; she outruns his horse and kills him, mocking his 'slippery native arts'.
body: The Ligurians of the north-western Apennines had a proverbial reputation for deceit: Servius quotes Cato's Origines, that they were unlettered and liars (mendaces), and Nigidius Figulus, who called them brigands and tricksters. Virgil introduces this one as 'not the meanest in Liguria while fate allowed him to deceive'. His challenge (fight on foot, not trusting your horse) is a trick, and Camilla punishes it by speed alone. Conington and Nettleship note that 'vane' may denote vain confidence or falsehood, that 'patrias' may refer to his country or to his father Aunus, and that 'lubricus' (slippery) is not elsewhere used by Virgil of moral deceit. The scene ends with a simile of a falcon, 'sacred bird', tearing a dove in the clouds, which Conington traces partly to Iliad 22.139-42 (Achilles chasing Hector like a falcon after a dove) and partly to Odyssey 15.525-8, where the falcon is Apollo's swift messenger.

title: Tarchon's taunt: Etruscan luxury
greek: at non in Venerem segnes nocturnaque bella, / aut ubi curva choros indixit tibia Bacchi, / exspectare dapes et plenae pocula mensae
short: The Etruscan leader shames his fleeing men: brave enough for love, Bacchic dances and banquets, but routed by a woman.
body: Tarchon's speech plays on the Roman stereotype of the Etruscans as lovers of pleasure: night-time 'wars of Venus', the curved Phrygian pipe (tibia) that summons Bacchic dances, rich feasts, and waiting for the soothsayer (haruspex) to announce a favourable sacrifice so that the fat victim may 'call them to the deep groves' for the sacrificial banquet. Conington and Nettleship explain the role of the pipe in sacrifice and its connection with Etruria, referring to Georgics 2.193 ('the fat Etruscan blew the ivory pipe at the altar'), and note with Servius that 'hic amor, hoc studium' (this your passion, this your desire) is a parenthesis. The taunt works: Tarchon seizes Venulus from his horse and carries him off like an eagle with a snake, a simile modelled on the eagle omen of Iliad 12.200-7.

title: Chloreus and Camilla's love of spoils
greek: caeca sequebatur totumque incauta per agmen / femineo praedae et spoliorum ardebat amore
short: Camilla blindly pursues Chloreus, Cybele's priest in gorgeous Phrygian armour, 'burning with a woman's love of booty and spoils', and so exposes herself to Arruns.
body: Chloreus is dressed in barbarian splendour: a horse in bronze scale armour, saffron and purple, a Lycian bow, a gold helmet, embroidered trousers. Virgil gives two possible motives for Camilla's pursuit: to hang Trojan arms in a temple, or to wear the captive gold herself. The phrase 'femineo amore' has been read as a misogynist judgement or, more often now, as part of a pattern in which desire for spoils is fatal: Euryalus dies after taking Messapus' helmet (9.359-66, 373-4) and Turnus after taking Pallas' belt (10.495-505, 12.941-9). Camilla's pursuit is 'caeca' and 'incauta', blind and careless, the moment Arruns has waited for. Servius glosses 'femineo' as impatient and irrational, and suggests that by attacking the priest of a greater deity (Cybele) Camilla forfeits Diana's protection. Chloreus survives the chase but is killed by Turnus in 12.363.

title: Apollo of Soracte and the fire-walkers
greek: summe deum, sancti custos Soractis Apollo, / quem primi colimus, cui pineus ardor acervo / pascitur, et medium freti pietate per ignem / cultores multa premimus vestigia pruna
short: Arruns prays to the Apollo of Mount Soracte, whose worshippers walked barefoot over burning pine embers at his festival.
body: Soracte is a solitary mountain north of Rome in Faliscan territory (the snow-capped peak of Horace, Odes 1.9). Its god was identified with Apollo (Soranus). Pliny the Elder reports that a few families called the Hirpi, at the annual sacrifice on Soracte, walked over a burnt pine-wood pyre without being scorched, and were for this reason exempted by the senate from military service (Natural History 7.19). Servius tells an aetiological story: wolves (Sabine hirpi) once snatched entrails from a sacrifice to Dis on the mountain, a plague followed, and an oracle said it would end if the people imitated wolves, that is, lived by plunder; hence the name Hirpi Sorani. Servius also comments that 'summe deum' expresses the worshipper's devotion, since strictly Jupiter is highest, and Conington and Nettleship take it to show that Apollo was the special god of Arruns' people.

title: Apollo grants half of Arruns' prayer
greek: audiit et voti Phoebus succedere partem / mente dedit, partem volucris dispersit in auras
short: Apollo lets Arruns kill Camilla but not return home; the other half of his prayer is scattered on the winds.
body: Arruns asks for no spoils or glory: only to kill 'this dread scourge' and go home 'inglorious'. The god grants the first half and lets the second blow away. The model is Iliad 16.249-52, where Zeus grants half of Achilles' prayer: Patroclus will drive the Trojans from the ships, but will not return safely. Arruns' modest prayer has struck readers as both cowardly and pathetic; Virgil shows him fleeing in terror after the throw, like a wolf that has killed a bullock and slinks off with its tail between its legs (11.809-13, after Iliad 15.585-90). The weapon strikes Camilla under the breast, 'and drank her maiden blood'. Opis' arrow then fulfils Diana's sentence on him.

title: Camilla's death: 'vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras'
greek: vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras
short: Camilla dies with a last message to Turnus; her life 'flees indignant to the shades', a line Virgil repeats as the last line of the whole poem.
body: Camilla's death is told with great tenderness: she pulls at the spear, her eyes and colour fade, and she sends her companion Acca with a last order for Turnus to take her place. The final line is repeated exactly at 12.952 for the death of Turnus. Conington and Nettleship note the repetition and record Servius' explanation that Camilla, like Turnus, dies young and therefore unwillingly ('indignata'); they compare Homer's lines on the deaths of Patroclus and Hector, whose souls fly to Hades 'lamenting their fate, leaving manhood and youth' (Iliad 16.855-7, 22.361-3). The repetition links the two great Italian defenders, both brave and both destroyed by the Trojans' destiny; it has been central to modern readings that hear in the poem's ending a note of grief as well as victory.

title: The tomb of Dercennus
greek: fuit ingens monte sub alto / regis Dercenni terreno ex aggere bustum / antiqui Laurentis opacaque ilice tectum
short: Opis takes her stand on the earthen burial mound of an ancient Laurentine king, shaded by holm-oak, to shoot Arruns.
body: Dercennus is otherwise unknown. Conington and Nettleship note that the only other notice is in Servius, who reports a view that the name was invented from that of Sterces (or Stercenius), a king of the Aborigines. A great earthen mound (agger) covering a royal grave belongs to the oldest Italian landscape that Virgil likes to evoke, with its sacred trees and tombs; the holm-oak (ilex) shading it is a typical funerary and sacred tree. Using an old king's tomb as the platform for divine vengeance gives the killing of Arruns a ritual setting: Camilla's slayer is shot from the grave of a native king and left unburied 'on the unknown dust of the plain', while Diana will carry Camilla's body home for burial (11.593-4).
